topic: tesla ai5 chip tapes out at samsung foundry, production soon
headline_marked: Tesla's AI5 chip [[tapes out at Samsung Foundry]] using 2nm-class node
headline: Tesla's AI5 chip tapes out at Samsung Foundry using 2nm-class node
summary: The AI5 processor, set for mass production, integrates a compact accelerator die with 12 SK hynix memory packages, potentially offering up to 1.5 TB/s bandwidth.
details: Tesla's AI5 chip has officially "taped out" at Samsung Foundry, utilizing the company's advanced 2nm-class process technology. This marks a significant step towards mass production for the processor, which is slated for integration into Tesla's next-generation products, including vehicles, robots, and data centers.

A principal engineer at Samsung Foundry confirmed the tape-out in a LinkedIn post, highlighting the collaboration with Tesla's engineering teams in Palo Alto and Austin. The AI5 chip was also taped out earlier at TSMC, with Samsung's version following months later.

The AI5 processor module features a compact accelerator die alongside 12 SK hynix memory packages. While the exact memory configuration isn't disclosed, the setup suggests a broad external memory interface, potentially reaching up to 1.536 TB/s if utilizing GDDR7 technology.

Elon Musk previously demonstrated a sample of the AI5, claiming it could deliver up to a 40X performance improvement over its predecessor in certain workloads. Tesla plans to produce AI5 in high volumes, leveraging both TSMC and Samsung Foundries to meet anticipated demand.

topic: state AGs sue to block paramount-warner bros discovery merger
headline_marked: [[12 States Sue]] to Block Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
headline: 12 States Sue to Block Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
summary: Attorneys general allege the $110 billion deal would violate antitrust laws by reducing competition in film distribution and cable channel licensing.
details: A dozen state attorneys general have filed an antitrust lawsuit in a bid to prevent Paramount from taking over Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD). The suit was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California.

The AGs allege that the merger would violate the Clayton Act by reducing competition among the distribution of wide-release theatrical films, distribution of anticipated top-grossing theatrical films, and licensing of basic cable channels to distributors.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta stated, "The unlawful merger of these two entertainment behemoths would lead to higher prices, lower quality and less content for film and television, harming movie theaters, basic cable distributors and ultimately, audiences."

The combined Paramount and WBD entity would account for 27 percent of the "wide-release theatrical distribution" market and three-tenths of "anticipated blockbuster films with wide audiences and large production budgets."
In terms of distributing basic cable channels, the two companies would make up a 27 percent share of the market, with WBD currently second and Paramount third.

A Paramount spokesperson called the lawsuit "fundamentally flawed" and stated, "We will vigorously defend the transaction and demonstrate that this challenge is inconsistent with sound competition policy."
Paramount argues the merger will create a stronger company better positioned to compete with streaming giants like Netflix, which has over 325 million subscribers globally.
The state AGs are expected to seek an injunction to block the deal from closing, though Paramount and WBD still need approval from regulators in other markets.
